utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like to start with the delivery of two decisions about which the parties are -- about which the parties are already informed. The first one is the decision in respect of protective measures for Witness 165. I'll deliver now the decision of -- of the Chamber on the Prosecution's application made in court last Friday for protective measures, that is, pseudonym, facial distortion, and partial private session for Witness 165. In its oral submissions last Friday, the Prosecution recalled the three-part test set out by this Chamber in its protective measures decision of the 22nd -- the 27th of April, 2005. In that decision, the Chamber stated that the existence of the requisite objectively grounded risk to the security of the witness or the witness's family can be demonstrated through a combination of the following three factors: (1) The expected testimony of the witness may antagonise persons who reside in the territory where the crimes were committed; for example, by implicating those persons in crimes; (2) The witness or his or her family live in that territory, have property in that territory, or have concrete plans to return to live in the territory; And, (3), there exists an unstable security situation, which is particularly unfavourable to witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. It was the Prosecution's submission that these three factors have been established in the case of Witness 165. The Defence, in its oral submissions, emphasised the fact that any risk to the security of the witness or the witness's family must be objectively grounded and submitted that the circumstances of Witness 165 do not meet the requisite standard. According to the Defence, if such circumstances were sufficient, protective measures would become the rule rather than the exception. The Chamber considers that its previous rulings have been clear on the question of what will be sufficient to show that an alleged risk to the security of a witness is objectively grounded. Without prejudice to situations falling outside the three-part test I have just recalled, that test was intended to give the parties a clear indication of one situation in which the Chamber will view an alleged security risk as being, in the words of the Defence, an "objective risk." In the case of Witness 165, the Chamber notes that his testimony concerns brutal and serious crimes allegedly committed by Serbs in the territory where members of the witness's family continue to reside, where the witness has property and to which the witness returns regularly. It is the Chamber's view that Witness 165's testimony may well antagonise persons living in that territory, which remains predominantly Serb, exposing the witness and his family to a security risk. Taking into account the UNHCR report of January 2005 to which the Prosecution referred and which this Chamber has accepted as demonstrating a climate unfavourable to those willing to testify before this Tribunal, the Chamber therefore considers that the Prosecution has met the requirements for the requested grant of protective measures in this case. The Chamber orders that Witness 165 testify under pseudonym, with facial distortion, and in private session for those portions of his testimony likely to reveal his identity. This concludes the Chamber's decision. The next decision I'd like to deliver is a -- is a decision on the seventh batch of 92 bis witnesses. I briefly recall that the Chamber is seized of two Prosecution motions for the admission of 92 bis evidence, filed on the 6th of June, 2003 (the seventh motion) and on the 9th of January, 2004 (the eighth motion). We are also seized of the Prosecution's fifteenth motion, dated the 20th of May, 2005, which consolidates the remaining 92 bis matters for the Prosecution's case. Madam Registrar, I'd like to ask you to hand out to the parties a list showing the names of the 92 bis witnesses and related material mentioned in the fifteenth motion which is admitted into evidence by virtue of today's decision. All of these witnesses are either protected or their status in this respect is as yet undetermined. This handout therefore is to be filed under seal. I will now deliver the Chamber's decision concerning these witnesses. There seems to be complete agreement between the parties on the material to be admitted. The Defence had only two requests in response to the Prosecution's fifteenth motion, one that it be supplied with the death certificates of the two deceased witnesses; the other that a redaction be made to the transcript evidence of Witness 545. The Prosecution has informed us by filing, dated the 10th of June, 2005, that it has complied with the request for the certificates and agreed -- agrees with the proposed redaction. The Chamber has, as usual, gone through all the proffered material, making its own assessment of the suitability of the material for admission. The Chamber finds, with one exception, that the material is suitable for admission under Rule 92 bis subject to the proposed redaction. The exception I've referred to concerns Witness 674. The fifteenth motion lists as the only item for admission a corrective statement dated 2003 to an original statement, not listed for admission, and as yet not in evidence, dated 1998. Without the original, the corrective statement cannot, of course, be admitted. The legal staff have informed the Prosecution of this apparent oversight, and follow-up action by the Prosecution has already been taken, as the Defence and the Chamber were informed by the Prosecution's e-mail dated the 30th of June, 2005. Unfortunately this means that the application concerning Witness 674 cannot be finalised with this decision. In conclusion, the material of the witnesses listed in the fifteenth motion, minus the redacted portion shown in the handout and minus the single item from 2003 for Witness 674, is hereby admitted. The Chamber requests that the Prosecution submit this material to Madam Registrar in due course. Madam Registrar will then assign exhibit numbers to these items and inform the parties and the Chamber. In addition to the outstanding matter of Witness 674, which I referred to above, another outstanding issue is the matter of protective measures - that is, pseudonym and concealment of identity from the public - of Witnesses 10 and 246 [sic]. The Prosecution will inform the Chamber and the Defence of its position in this respect after it has made contact with the witnesses' families. The Prosecution should endeavour to have this matter settled in advance of the 22nd of July. In the meantime, Witnesses 2 -- 10 and 426 will be referred to by their witness codes. This ends the Chamber's decision on the seventh batch of 92 bis witnesses. Then is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's Witness 165.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Protective measures as just set out in our decision -- the public gallery is empty, which means that the witness can be brought into the courtroom without any risk for being recognised. The technical staff is instructed, I take it, to take care that the face of the witness does not appear. Mr. Usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, while that's happening, just an area where I would be seeking Your Honours' guidance, and that's with respect to proposed contextual documents, a batch of which have already been admitted to evidence and have received P numbers, which I would like to refer the Trial Chamber to, as they might be of assistance. And a small number of additional documents - I think a total of six - which have not yet received numbers. They would be new documents. And I'm wondering if Your Honours would -- if your preference would be to deal with that before the witness begins his testimony or at the conclusion of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Numbers will be assigned when the documents are shown to the witness, and we'll then decide at the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, the documents I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not going to show them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, these are contextual documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Contextual, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The potential exhibits to be shown to the witness himself are a small number of photographs, which he will comment on. But these contextual documents are ones which the Prosecution feels would assist all the parties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have expressed a preference for contextual documents to be presented when the witness is there, at least in the context of his -- of his testimony so that we don't have to wait. At the same time, these contextual documents are more or less dossier documents as well. We also have to keep in mind that we do not, through this split-up system of contextual documents and dossiers, make the number of documents even higher. But we'll deal with it after the witness has given his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just prior to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Just prior to the usher bringing the witness into the courtroom, there was also a matter that I wanted to raise just prior to the -- the witness being brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, next time -- the witness is now half in, half out. Could you announce that a bit earlier so that we avoid this rather embarrassing situation with the witness. But please -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Very brief, Your Honour. Your Honours, just in relation to that decision on 674, I can indicate that I think originally the Prosecution had intended to tender some transcript, and I just foreshadow that it's -- it may be likely that the Defence might wish to introduce some of that transcript. That's it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that information. Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness, Witness 165, because that's how we are going to address you. Witness 165, before you give evidence, you're required to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Witness 165.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would just like you to know that your face cannot be seen by the outside world. We'll not use your name. We'll call you "Witness 165." And if there will be any portion of your evidence that could identify you, then we'll turn into private session so that those portions of the evidence cannot be heard by anyone outside this courtroom. You'll first be examined by Ms. Edgerton, counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If Witness 165 could be given the pseudonym sheet, please. If it could be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be Prosecution Exhibit P859, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness 165, good morning. You --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You have a piece of paper in front of you which bears a name and date of birth on that. Could you have a look at that piece of paper for us and tell us if that information relates to you and the information is correct. Is that your name and your date of birth on the piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could next refer to the witness's previous statement to the Office of the Prosecutor and that could be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Prosecution Exhibit P860, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could the witness receive a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Witness 165, have you had during the course of your preparation for testimony today a chance to review that statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And does the translation correspond with what was read back to you in 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise your signature on the original English language document which was read back to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't hear a translation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, subject to some corrections contained in a separate document, do you find this statement to be substantially correct and an accurate reflection of your recollection of what you saw, heard, and experienced in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now if we could refer to the supplementary information report which was signed by the witness, and if it could be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P861, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. And if you could just assist the witness by turning to that document in the batch of materials he has before him. And I do note that as of now there is no translation into B/C/S of the document the witness has before him because he prepared it late yesterday afternoon, but we should be able to provide one before court concludes this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Witness 165, have you had this document read back to you in your own language in preparation for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And does this document accurately reflect the corrections and clarifications you wish to make to your statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'll begin. And I would ask that you keep this statement -- a copy of the statement in front of you for the time being because, Witness 165, as I ask you questions, I'm going to be referring you to paragraphs which you'll see are numbered in your statement that you gave in 1996. Can we just go first, Witness 165, to paragraph 8 of your previous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, do I understand -- I was under the impression that you'd use the 89(F) procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've done it again, Your Honour. Yes, and I'll read the 89(F) summary at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you explained to the witness what it means?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour. And the witness has also had an opportunity to listen to the 89(F) summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In his own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you have been informed by Ms. Edgerton that we do not require you to repeat everything you said already in your statement. But for the public to know what is -- what are -- is the content of your written statement, a summary will be read out, and then further questions will be put to you. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And my apologies. The witness is a Muslim from a village in Zvornik municipality in Bosnia. He's married with three children. Prior to the war, the witness's village was almost 100 per cent Muslim. Having heard stories of the crimes perpetrated by Arkan's men in Bijeljina and expecting the Serbs would continue their path of violence into Eastern Bosnia, the people of the witness's village organised to defend themselves. The witness had a clear view of what was happening in Zvornik during the attack and takeover of the town. Early one morning, about a month after Zvornik fell, the witness heard by loudspeaker that Kula Grad had fallen and the people of his village were given an ultimatum to surrender by 9.00 a.m. that day. About one half hour before the ultimatum was to expire, the witness's village was shelled, and the shelling continued for the next eight hours. At dawn the next morning, people were ordered out of their houses to a local hotel. The village had been entered by Arkanovci, Seseljevci, and Beli Orlovi. The villagers were returned to their houses after a period of time, but it was made clear to them by Serb forces that they could not leave the village. The witness describes looting of village homes over the next weeks by Arkan's forces. Villagers were told that apart from looting, nothing would happen to them and they would be safe. The witness reports that one Major Pavlovic came to the villagers and personally guaranteed their safety. On 26 May 1992, however, Pavlovic returned and said that even though he had done his utmost to protect the villagers, they now had to leave and transport would be arranged for them. They were told they Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were being taken to Bosnian-held territory. A short time later, between four and five hundred villagers were taken in nine buses to Pogled near Han Pijesak. There they were stopped by Serbs, who told them they couldn't go any further. The Serbs used the prisoners and their buses as human shields for an advance of their front line. Early on 27 May, the detainees were told they weren't able to cross to Bosnian-held territory, as they had planned, but that they were to be taken to Tuzla. The buses travelled to Zvornik, where they were joined by 15 to 20 women and children, and then they travelled to Crni Vrh, where they used again as human shields to advance the front line. After this, the detainees were all driven back to Zvornik, where the men were ordered to leave the buses and go into the local football stadium. They were held at gunpoint on the grandstands, and from the stadium the men were taken to a building, where they remained for two days. On the first day, they were seen by Brano Grujic, who told the detainees they had to list themselves and that he would arrange for them to sign loyalty to the Serb authorities, after which they would be taken to their village and released. He told them he would get food to them. They never saw Grujic again, nor did they receive any food. The list was completed; there were 186 men. After the second day, the detainees were taken to the Dom Kulture in Celopek. They were guarded by Serb police. The prisoners were held there in a single room which had a stage at one end. For three days they received no food or water. On the third day, when they began to receive food, the beatings started. Paramilitary groups started to arrive at any time of the day or night. The witness heard the members of these groups speaking to one another and recognised them as coming from Serbia. From what the witness heard, he concluded one group was led by a man called Dusan Repic; another was made by somebody called Major Toro, and in his group were people with nicknames such as Zoks, Pufte, and Niski. The witness talks in great detail about the extreme beatings and torture the detainees in Celopek were subject to. People were randomly executed, sometimes summarily, sometimes in brutal fashion. Some of the incidents are described in this summary. On 11 June 1992 at about 2.00 a.m., Repic and his men came to the Dom Kulture and said they wanted to celebrate Bajram in a bloody way. They took pairs of fathers and sons onto the stage in the room and forced them to perform fellatio on one another. Two of these prisoners had their penises cut off. They and others were forced to eat them. Some of these victims were slaughtered. Prisoners had their fingers amputated. Repic was in charge of the whole operation. He had a desk that he would call people up to. Repic was armed with a small-calibre rifle. The witness saw Repic use this rifle to shoot four men at close range. They were so close to the witness he was sprayed with blood. That same night, Repic and his men picked out the witness's oldest brother for beating. The man the witness knew as Pufte beat the witness's brother with, among other things, a chair. The brother eventually died from his injuries on 15 June 1992. He never received medical help. On 27 June 1992, Repic arrived at Celopek alone, armed with an automatic rifle. He ordered prisoners to line up in rows of three and began shooting them one by one. At one point, while actually talking with the witness, other prisoners surrounded Repic. He panicked and broke away, ordering the prisoners to line up against the wall. He emptied his gun, an automatic rifle, into the crowd. Twenty people were killed, another twenty-two wounded. The men were eventually transferred to the Zvornik local court building, thanks, the witness later learned, to the intervention of some Serb women with Grujic. There were 104 detainees left by this time. Conditions were cramped. They slept in shifts. Beatings there continued. After two weeks, the men were told they were going to a better place and were loaded onto buses and sent to Batkovic detention facility. There were about 1.600 prisoners there. The witness notes where they were from. The prisoners at Batkovic were sporadically beaten by the guards. From Batkovic, the witness was sent to do forced labour, from working in the fields to working on the front line. This included working in freezing conditions from October 1992 through January 1993. The witness was eventually exchanged on 21 July 1993. And that concludes the summary of the witness's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Witness 165, having read the summary of the written evidence that you previously gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, I'll begin again with asking you a number of questions based on or drawn from what you set out in your previous statement. If you could have a look at paragraph 8 of your previous statement just to place things a bit more precisely in time. Does this paragraph actually relate to events in very late March and early April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that only a few days before the attack on Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Zvornik fell -- please could you rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 of your previous statement refers to people of your village arming themselves in defence. How long before the attack on Zvornik did that take place? A short time or a long time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: A short time before the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In this same paragraph, you mention receiving 25 automatic rifles and a machine-gun from the Zvornik SUP. How did that come about? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: The SUP was divided. So there were 25 automatic rifles and one machine-gun that were provided, one part.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And one part being what? Could you just be a bit more precise so we all understand you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: The regular police force before the war broke out was divided into Serbian and Muslim parts, since the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been recognised. So the SUP was divided and 25 automatic rifles and one machine-gun were provided to us by the regular authorities, whereas the other side held onto the other equipment. We used those weapons to erect defence positions along the axis routes to the village of Divic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge, was -- could you tell us whether or not there was ever any organised supply of weapons to your village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we turn next to paragraphs 9 in your previous statement through to paragraph 12. Those paragraphs, from what I understand by reading, talk about a series of three negotiations between Muslims and Serbs over the fate of your village. Now, could you tell us: Are these meetings set out in your statement in the chronicle order as they happened? Chronological order.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us, did these meetings take place before or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's rephrase -- let me re-put these last two questions so that we hear the answers. Are these meetings set out in your statement in the chronological order in which they took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did these meetings take place before or after the attack on Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: After the attack on Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in the negotiations talked about in paragraph 9, could you tell us, how did you yourself come to learn what Halilovic had been told?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: At a gathering in the place, in the village, Halilovic appeared at that gathering and he quite literally said that the inhabitants would come to no harm if we signed a pledge of loyalty to the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At that time -- do you recall whether at that time Halilovic told the people who were gathered who on the Serb side he had been in contact with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: He said he had been in contact with Major Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move to paragraph -- the second set of negotiations mentioned in paragraph 10 in your previous statement, and I'd like to ask you: How did you learn what was said at these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: I heard about it at the gathering in the village when the then-representative of Zvornik municipality appeared and the representative of the Zvornik municipality Territorial Defence. They appeared at the stadium. The negotiations had been taking place at the power plant. There were negotiations with Arkan and his men. They said that they had not been successful and that they had fled from that place, and as a result we had to establish a Crisis Staff again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's move to paragraph 11, going through your statement. Could you just tell us exactly where Kula Grad is in relation to your village and the city of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Kula Grad is on an elevation. My place is to the right, Zvornik to the left, and the power plant -- the Zvornik power plant is in the middle. From Kula Grad, there is an excellent view of my village. You can see the entire power plant. You can see Mali Zvornik, which is in Serbia, and you can see part of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how did you come to go up to Kula Grad, as you talk about in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: I went to Kula Grad with another man to check the situation since Zvornik had already fallen and it was a vital point. It was a -- an important position that couldn't easily be taken. I observed what was happening in Zvornik from Kula Grad, and I observed the movement of other paramilitary formations, their movement from Mali Zvornik -- or in Mali Zvornik and in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in relation, then, to what you could see, could you tell us whether you saw from this view any military presence in the area in addition to the paramilitaries, any -- any armament, for example.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: There were weapons at the power plant. There were -- there was a anti-aircraft machine-gun. There were tanks. But it was all on the Serbian side, on the side of Republika Srpska. And that is the position from which my town, my village was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could move forward, then, in time to the third set of negotiations that you seem to be describing in paragraph 12. Do you know who on the Muslim side was involved in these last negotiations you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: I don't know if I can mention any names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness can mention names. So you may do so. I -- unless you'd consider that by mentioning those names in this context that you would reveal your own identity, because that's protected, not the identity of others. But if it would be so close, if you would be the one who would know those names and others would not and therefore you might identify yourself, then we could turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary. I can mention their names. These were inhabitants from my village who were in the Crisis Staff. There was Rasim Zahirovic and Rasim Tabic. They were the last men to be involved in negotiations with Arkan and his men, and these negotiations took place at the power plant, once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not those negotiations were successful?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: When they returned, they told us that the negotiations had not been successful. An ultimatum had been issued according to which by 9.00 on the following day the weapons were to be surrendered to the Serbian authorities. If they weren't surrendered by that time, the village would be attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just prior to Ms. Edgerton proceeding with the next question, I might indicate that there does appear to be a -- a mistranslation at page 19, line 9 that might have to be clarified. That's just in the -- you know, "That it was all on the Serbian side, on the side of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I wondered -- it came into my mind whether there was any mistake there because, of course, it was just at the border of Serbia. So could you please identify -- please clarify whether -- whether there's any confusion about Serbian side, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness 165, can we just go back to your answers to the questions about what you saw from the view at Kula Grad. You offered to the Court that the armaments that you saw were positioned in Serbia and in Republika Srpska. Could you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, that's not quoting correctly what's on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you said you could see those weapons, and you said where they were located. They were at the other side. Could you tell us whether you meant to say at the territory held by the other forces or on the territory of Serbia proper? So the other side of the river. Could you tell us what you meant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the other side of the river. That's where an anti-aircraft machine cannons were located, and this belonged to the regular army of the Republic of Serbia and they shelled Kula Grad from that position, and the regular army also used those weapons to subsequently shell my village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that is now clear. Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Going back to where we left off, we left off at the delivery of the ultimatum, and that takes us to paragraph 14 of your previous statement and the attack on your village. Are you able to tell us, because according to your statement you were in your village, from which direction the shelling then came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: The shelling came from the direction of the Republic of Serbia. I was shelled by the regular army of the then-JNA of the Republic of Serbia. Some of them were at the power plant and others were on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: After the shelling of your village had come to an end, could you tell us how you were ordered out of your house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: A loudspeaker that was at the power plant was used to order us to go towards the Vidikovac Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'd like to move now to a question in relation to paragraph 15 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in anticipation of what might come and the answer, I'd ask that we move to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Going forward now, Witness 165, to paragraph 16 of your statement. Could I ask you to turn to paragraph 16. Do you see paragraph 16 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You note a Major Pavlovic came to you and personally guaranteed your safety. Did you actually hear this Major Pavlovic say this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes, I heard him say that. That was at the gathering at the stadium. Pavlovic appeared in front of a mass of people. He said that nothing would happen to us. He said that we'd sign a pledge of loyalty to the Serbian authorities and that we would remain in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how did you come to be gathered at the stadium on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Well, Halilovic Mirsad, who has already been mentioned, and he had contact with Major Pavlovic. He and some other young men went from house to house and called the people to assemble at the stadium where this meeting was to take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was this the first time you ever laid eyes on Major Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How was he dressed at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: He was wearing the uniform of the regular JNA, an officer's uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could move still forward, to paragraph 18 of your previous statement, when you speak about being rounded up in front of the mosque and threatened with being shot. Could you tell us approximately when this incident took place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: A meeting was held in front of the mosque. Someone called Rambo appeared. This meeting had previously been announced, and some paramilitary formations surrounded us, so he said that we should surrender all our weapons. We hadn't surrendered our weapons. We practically had no weapons. And as a result he said that he had to sign a document stating that the village was not completely cleansed of weapons and he said, "May Allah help you?" He said he had to sign this document for his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Witness 165, I'd like you to probably try and look at me a bit more and be guided by the question that I ask you, because the information that you've given just now is actually information that's contained in your previous statement and in the corrections that you made. The question I'd like to know is: Approximately -- do you remember approximately when this happened? Or if I could help you by asking another way: Do you remember approximately how long after the attack on your village this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: A few days earlier, six or seven days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember how you were called out to be gathered at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Some inhabitants went from house to house and summoned the men, asked them to go to the mosque. They said that there would be a meeting in front of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. I -- I'd just like to go back again --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go back again just to the answer to your question -- or to my question about approximately when you were gathered at the mosque. Your answer was six or seven days before the attack on your village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: After the attack. The village had already been attacked. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's go to paragraph 19 of your statement. And at this paragraph, you talk about seeing Major Pavlovic again on 26 May 1992. Was this actually when you first heard that you were going to be moved out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: I heard that a day before Major Pavlovic appeared at the stadium. It was at a gathering in front of the bakery. Mirsad Halilovic had organised that gathering and Zucanin [phoen] -- was also there -- Zuco's men were there in camouflage uniforms. They said we had to move out. We didn't move out that day; we moved out on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The following day being the day at which you saw Major Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where was this meeting where you saw him the following day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: He was in front of the stadium -- on the ground in front of the stadium in my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how did you come to be assembled at that meeting in front of the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Well, as they had done before, they went from house to house and told the people that they had to go to the stadium. They said that there were buses waiting and that we had to move out. When we arrived at the stadium, there were buses waiting for us there. There were nine Drinatrans buses from Zvornik that were waiting there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So how long were you given to pack up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Would it be correct only pack the essential things we had, some clothes of ours, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I take it from your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. There's something I would like to understand. In your statement and in the course of your testimony today, you have mentioned the presence of paramilitary groups but also the presence of the so-called regular army, because you say that Major Pavlovic was a member of the JNA. I would like you to explain to us whether these forces were together. I'd like you to tell us whether these forces acted in concert. Were JNA members a group that was different from the members of paramilitary groups, or did they form a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we're referring to the JNA and Major Pavlovic, well, he introduced himself as a JNA officer, an officer of the regular army, and there were no other units with him. He acted independently. He provided protection for our place. But when I previously mentioned units of the regular JNA, I was referring to the Republic of Serbia, to a different state. So we are confusing two separate things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this major, he was isolated from the JNA at that point in time. He was in the village itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He would occasionally come to the village, but I don't know where he'd be -- when it was necessary for him to come to the village, he would come, but he would come to provide protection for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at the time of the negotiations, there were paramilitary members, not just members of the military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say that this major, Major Pavlovic, was there to protect you, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It means that nothing would happen to us while he was there because paramilitary groups had already taken over power in Zvornik itself. Zvornik fell and they assumed power there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when he said he would provide you with protection, protection against whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, protection against paramilitary formations: Arkan's men, Seselj's men, the White Eagles. It didn't last for long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when he came to negotiate, you say that he came alone, without his unit. He was the only member of the military with you. He wasn't accompanied by members of paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said in your statement that on the 26th of May, 1992 Major Pavlovic: "[In English] Once again came and told us that although he had done his utmost to protect us, the time had come," and so on. [Interpretation] He said he did his utmost to protect you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and that there was nothing else he could do. And as Mirsad Halilovic said on that same occasion, that he was under threat and that his life was in danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to Major Pavlovic. He used to tell you that he had done his utmost in order to protect you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not directly. Indirectly. This information was given to us through Mirsad Halilovic, who was the person appointed as a contact person for any talks with Major Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one additional question in this respect. When he said that he could not protect you anymore, if your statement you say that he told you - that's Major Pavlovic - that you had to leave the village and that transport would be arranged for you and that nine buses later arrived. Do you know who arranged for that transport, who arranged for these nine buses that arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The day before, at the meeting, paramilitary formations, headed by Zuco, they chased us and then they came back on the next day and the buses were already waiting, and Zuco's forces made us board the buses under duress, and Major Pavlovic was there in the beginning and then he vanished, and then he talked to us about the situation and he said that he was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That does not entirely answer my question. I do understand that both the paramilitaries and Major Pavlovic were aware, observed the buses to arrive. Have you -- was it the paramilitaries that organised those buses or was it Major Pavlovic or someone else, or have you any idea on -- on who? I mean, nine buses usually do not just come from the air. Someone must have organised it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about it, but the buses were waiting for us at the stadium. As to who organised the buses to come and pick us up and relocate us, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what was your impression? Who finally said that you all had to leave your village? Was it Major Pavlovic who said, "I can't further protect you; therefore you have to leave," or was it the paramilitaries who said, "We don't need you anymore; you have to leave"? What, in your view, caused you to leave? Who put pressure upon it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have -- in addition to what you've heard, Witness 165, a few more questions about that meeting. First of all - and I think you've mentioned this before - what kind of buses were those that were waiting for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Those were Drinatrans Zvornik buses. And I used to take a bus like that before the war on a regular basis to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you see who drove these buses that you boarded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: The drivers who used to drive them before when I took them to go to work, and there were some others that I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I take it from reference to "guards" in another paragraph of your statement that in addition to the drivers, who you've just said were regular Drinatrans drivers, there -- there were guards on each bus. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It really is preferable that -- if there isn't leading, if the witness's voice comes out as opposed to "I take it from references," and what have you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. You're invited to lead not in the way you did by Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, in paragraph 23 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness meanwhile answered the question, so therefore, I don't know whether it's any need -- I didn't understand it to be an invitation to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, it certainly isn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But I would invite Ms. Edgerton to ensure that that no longer occurs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These guards that were on the bus, did you see what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms. Those were Zuco's people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the last sentence. Could the witness speak closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are invited to come a bit closer to the microphone because the witnesses [sic] have difficulties in hearing you at the same time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, one last question with respect to paragraph 19. You note that you and your buses were used as human shields in an advance, but you don't describe how this happened in that paragraph. Could you tell us now how you were used as human shields.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: When we boarded the bus, we set off. And in the area of Han Pijesak there were tanks and heavy artillery preceding us by about a kilometre and we followed on those buses, and then we also spent the night on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In paragraph 21, you say that you were again used as human shields at a location called Crni Vrh. First of all, where is Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Crni Vrh is about 20 kilometres away from Zvornik in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how on this second occasion were you used as human shields, as you've described -- or as you mentioned in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: In the same way as before, in the area of Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to paragraph 25 and at that point we're dealing with your return to Zvornik and your stay in the Novi Izvor building. Could you tell us how you were escorted from the stadium into the Novi Izvor building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: We went in a column of four holding hands, from the stadium to the Novi Izvor building, and we were flanked by police from the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I do note the time, Your Honour. Could I have some guidance as to when you'd like to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We usually have a break at 10.30. If this would be a suitable moment, we could -- we could take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would only have two more questions, Your Honour, and then -- we would take us another two minutes and then lead us right to 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You say in this paragraph 25 that Brano Grujic came to Novi Izvor and told you to do certain things and promised you certain things. How did you recognise the person you've said was Brano Grujic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Because I knew him in person.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were you under guard while you stayed at Novi Izvor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes. Reserve police officers kept guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe now, Your Honour, it would be a suitable time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Edgerton, could you also give us for scheduling purposes, give us an impression on how much time you would need in total? You spent now a little bit over one hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I -- your indulgence for just a moment, please. After the break, perhaps -- I think no more than one further hour, Your Honour. Perhaps less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We'll have a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom, as the public gallery is empty, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, as we move on to the next areas of questioning, I think it's going to be prudent that we also move into private session and remain in private session for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness 165, I'd like to move forward in time to paragraph 43 of your statement that you gave to the OTP, and that deals with your transfer from Celopek to the court building in Zvornik. Do you know where the court building was in relation to the municipality headquarters building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes. It was about 15 or 20 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How were you moved from Celopek to the court building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: We were moved in Drinatrans Zvornik buses, and this time we were escorted by the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And while you were held at the court building, were you under guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Yes, we were guarded by the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How did you come to learn about -- as you say in paragraph 43, how did you come to learn that local Serb women after the Vidovdan incident had gone to see Grujic to protest that people from Divic had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: I found out about that after a long period of time, when I was moved to the Batkovic camp. Other Muslims who were detained with me told me about that, but they had arrived later on. They were still in Zvornik and they said that they were looting other houses for paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we move forward, then, to paragraph 48 of your statement, and that deals with the transfer to Batkovic. Could you tell us how you were moved to Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: We were moved to Batkovic in Drinatrans buses, and there were members of paramilitary formations in uniform with us, two in each bus, and there was also a line-up of the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, a line-up of the reserve police force where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: From the building where we were detained, the former court building, up -- as far as the buses. There were two lines with five metres in between each of them, two lines of the reserve police force. We got on the buses. We didn't know where we were going, but later we found out that we had arrived in the village of Batkovic. We had arrived at a farm.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You mentioned that 22 wounded had been moved from Celopek to the courthouse in Zvornik, but I wonder if you know what happened to those 22 after you were transferred to Batkovic. Did they go to Batkovic with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Those wounded individuals stayed on in the building. They remained in the building, and we went to Batkovic and we heard nothing about them afterwards. Later on a neighbour who had been detained with them arrived. He arrived in Batkovic and he said that they had all gone in the direction of -- left in the direction of Olovo-Kladanj for an exchange, but they have all disappeared without a trace.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my questions for Witness 165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Ms. Loukas, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just some material that I'll need to check prior to the -- the commencement of my cross-examination. I can indicate my cross-examination won't be very long, but I -- I'd like to check this material prior to the commencement. I'm just wondering if we could perhaps take an early break or what have you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But thinking of breaks and scheduling, would the next witness be available for the Prosecution? I wonder whether ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I take it the next witness would be available tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How much time do you think you'd need, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've just received a note that I need to look at. I mean, we can either -- you can either give me, I don't know, ten minutes, Your Honour, or -- or we can take the break now and then proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if -- if you would not need much time -- I understand it to be not more than 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that correct? Yes. Then perhaps we have a very short -- we'll give you the ten minutes now and not have the break, because that would finally result in a later moment where we can conclude this morning's session.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then have a break for ten minutes. If you'd need more time, Ms. Loukas, would you please take care that we are informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn -- we'll resume at ten minutes to 12.00. --- Break taken at 11.39 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, are you ready to cross-examine the witness? If he's in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once he's in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, once he's in the courtroom, then I'm ready to cross-examine him, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Usher, could you please escort him into the courtroom. The public gallery is empty; is that correct? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 165, you'll now be examined by Ms. Loukas, counsel for the Defence. The Chamber observed and noticed that giving this testimony is quite emotional for you. Whenever you think you'd need more time, please ask for it and take your time. Ms. Loukas, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I just want to echo the -- the words that have been indicated by His Honour to you. And I echo as Defence counsel should you at any time need a break or what have you, please inform the Court. Now, what I also want to make clear to you, just to make you comfortable, is that I won't be asking any questions about the appalling events that you've given evidence of, but I'd like to ask you some surrounding questions. I take it you understand the -- the approach that I've just outlined?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you understood what Ms. Loukas said to you, that she'll not put questions to you on the appalling events but some questions -- some surrounding questions? Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, just in relation to the -- this man that you've given evidence in relation to, the man called Repic, his full name, of course, is Dusan Vukovic; correct? Vuckovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but they called him Dusan Repic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, are you aware that, in fact, Mr. Repic has been sentenced in Serbia for matters of the nature of which you've given evidence of? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: I have some knowledge about the fact, and I've been told that he has been convicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that matter can be confirmed by the -- the Prosecution in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, is that confirmed?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm -- I'm in possession of an indictment against Mr. Dusko Vuckovic for a number, not all, of the crimes that arose from Celopek. I can confirm, but I'd have to consult with a colleague outside of the courtroom, whether or not he's in fact been sentenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Loukas, a very -- perhaps a very technical question: Is this a final judgement?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I -- I, in fact, did not have any material from the Prosecution in relation to this question. I asked my case manager to perform an Internet search in relation to these matters confirming that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you by any way happen to know what the punishment imposed was?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There is an article in the newspaper in Belgrade of July the 12th, 2001 that indicates ten years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, were you aware, Witness, that this man was diagnosed as a severe psychopath?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 165
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, just going on to another matter. Just in relation to -- of course, you gave a statement to the -- the Prosecution that is an exhibit before the Court. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We now are in open session again. Witness 165 has finished his testimony and is excused. Ms. Edgerton, I take it that you'd like to discuss briefly the contextual exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, you've seen the list. I think the usual way of dealing with it is that you get one week to oppose. If --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And these documents are, of course, in addition to the -- the dossier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In -- to the Zvornik dossier, yes. I would have one question at this moment, Ms. Edgerton - and perhaps draw at the same time the attention of the Defence to it - I see that there are two interviews on the list, Dusko Vuckovic -- usually statements are introduced either through 92 bis or 89(F) or in special circumstances through expert report. Here I see that -- of course, we have not seen it yet, but is there any explanation for not following the 92 bis or -- I can imagine the specific position of this person has played a role.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, it does and has, Your Honour. And just to put those two proposed contextual documents in context. When Mr. Hannis tendered P780, which is one of the contextual documents I would refer the Trial Chamber to that's already been entered into evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- that was in his examination-in-chief of the Witness Davidovic. And when he tendered that document, he indicated to the parties he was also tendering 17 statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Which were translated up to that point. There was just -- that's 17 from a total of 65. He also stated the Prosecution's intention was to complete the translations of those documents and review their contents and perhaps consider tendering them through a later witness, 682, or in the Zvornik dossier. But because of the particular position of these two individuals who gave these statements vis-a-vis the witness's testimony, I thought it more useful to the parties to draw the parties' attention to those two at this time rather than at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a look at it and we'll also have a look at the relation, 92 bis and 89(F) and this non-92 bis, non-89(F) introduction. I'd like to very briefly deal with a few procedural matters. First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, you have presented some documents. The cover page will first be -- that's in relation to witnesses that have already -- that testified already. The cover pages will first be translated. Then we'll deal with it once we have access to that. So we'll come back to that. That's one thing. Then there is another matter. Let me just find it. Yes. In relation - and this is new - in the sixth batch of 92 bis material, the Chamber said that it was a bit uncertain in respect of witness or expert Kaiser, what portions of his transcript were tendered because there were no highlights in it. We have not been fully consistent in that decision because a similar problem, although not entirely -- not exactly the same, is true for Mr. Wright. There's one transcript where only a few pages are highlighted and there's another transcript where there are no pages highlighted at all. The Chamber would also here like to know whether that second -- of that second transcript, without any highlighting, whether that is a mistake or whether you'd just say it's there but nothing is standard, because there's no highlights, or that it is just the other way around, that everything is standard because there are no highlights. We'd like to hear about that. And then finally, I do understand that in relation to the expert Nielsen that where the Chamber has invited the Prosecution to -- to review the relevance of -- especially of those documents that were not used, and I also do understand that such a review has taken place. Has it been discussed already with the Defence so that the Chamber can be informed about to what extent there's any dispute about what should and what should not be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. My understanding was that the Court would first make a determination about whether or not those submitted documents fell within the Court's guidelines and then the Defence would have a chance to respond to -- if it felt that any of those documents were for some reason not properly admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can imagine why you'd think that, but I think the best way -- I mean, even a determination whether these documents fall within the guidelines of the Chamber, yes or no, is something which is a matter for -- could be a matter of dispute. So therefore the Chamber would prefer to -- to -- that the OTP informs the Defence what conclusions they have reached as far as relevance, et cetera, and then inform the Chamber whether there's any remaining dispute about that. And, of course, the final determination whether the Chamber accepts that or not is of course in our hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll take the first opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to the contextual documents, I have been reminded that with those that have already received an exhibit number should be read onto the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd rather not deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have to deal with that tomorrow. I'm aware also that it's not very convenient for you because you might have to come back to court. But if there's no disagreement, then -- about it, then it might not even be necessary for you to return; although, you're always -- we like to see you come into court, Ms. Edgerton. Ms. Loukas, you as well, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. I'm very happy for that, Your Honour. I might indicate that I've -- I've got copies of that particular statement that I was cross-examining on in both English and B/C/S. And I should also place on the record that the printer wasn't working in the Defence room this morning, and Ms. Edgerton very kindly - and we're most appreciative of that - gave us her English copy so we could photocopy it for the Court's benefit, which makes proceedings a lot more efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's always good to hear that. Cooperation is good. At least, I'd like to assign D numbers to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, out of an abundance of caution, we see that this, of course, could confuse, that the institute also provided a pseudonym to the -- to the witness, which of course --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is a different one than we use. It's a non-signed statement. Let's do it the following way: We assign a -- an exhibit number to it. It seems that the witness at least confirmed that he has spoken to people. If there's any objection, the OTP, the Office of the Prosecution, might take one or two days to -- to see whether the -- the fact that the statement is not signed is -- causes any problem. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understood it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- there was no objection. I don't know if the Prosecution needs two days and the matter can be settled at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Well, let's just say we provisionally admit it into evidence but the Prosecution -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under seal, yes. That's because, of course, we find a lot of information in the statement that might be --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that other material - and I note the time and I'm sure everybody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- the interpreters and the staff outside the courtroom are probably anxious to finish the session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other Chambers who want to sit perhaps. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The only other aspect, of course, is that material in relation to the man Repic. And I can now -- I can tender that actual article that I referred to as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I do understand. Nevertheless, in order to avoid that we get all kind of different information, like the rape was in this context, was not in the context, he got ten years, he got 15 years that, the parties first try to find out what relevant facts are agreed upon. Then inform the Chamber about it. And I think if you agree, it's -- it's not in the core of the case. It's not -- it's just background.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do agree, the Chamber could just accept that. And if we need any further documentation, we'll ask for it. And if the parties would agree that it would be helpful to already have the documentation - for example, by one translation, a copy of the judgement or whatever - then we'll hear from the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And just one final matter very quickly, Your Honour. I just want to ensure through Your Honour that if -- if there is material of this sort, that the Prosecution does provide it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will, as we have in the past, endeavour to be of as much assistance as possible. These are public documents, however, and it doesn't obviate the obligation of the Defence to engage in their own efforts to find and locate and use documents which are readily available to both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, as I said before, I used the very cautious expression that these documents tend to be not unfavourable to the Defence, so they could -- and to what extent they're public is -- is sometimes uncertain. I mean, if it is on the Internet, from what I understand, then first I can imagine that you'd rather have it verified as to the quality of the document, what's comment, what's -- what's a authentic document. So therefore I'm a bit cautious at this moment to say that in respect of this material, that it's just public documents, and I carefully listen to you, Mr. Tieger. I also heard you say - which is perhaps even more important - that the OTP does it utmost best always to assist the Defence in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just trying to strike the right balance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've done that for you. Yes, then numbers for the ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be Defence document number D45, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then not one word of apology but I should spend at least 25 words of apology to the technical staff and the interpreters for this late finish today. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of July, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.04 p.m.,
